interpretation.statusMeans: Engineering disposition for this exact source clause. DONE is scoped existing behavior; READY is local authorized work, including a precise design/profile artifact where wire details are absent; BLOCKED names missing implementation contract/tool/predecessor or an explicit qualification-only row. Qualification/activation is tracked separately.
interpretation.readinessIsNotTaskAdmission: P-* and L-* are proposals; tasks/todo.md is authoritative for T IDs, owner assignment and current progress. Active T33–T41 are not marked DONE here.
interpretation.noDuplicateWork: Repeated source clauses retain every source location and canonicalRequirementGroup/duplicateExecutionOf; common behavior/task references identify one execution task. Alias tasks are omitted from canonicalTasks.
interpretation.requirementsGranularity: Every non-metadata technical paragraph, bullet/ordered bullet, table data/header row and code-contract block is indexed; prose is split into source clauses. Link-only bibliography/catalog items and examples are not claimed as independently passed tests. Code fields belonging to one versioned API remain one contract requirement.
interpretation.sourceInspection: Actual packages/apps/contracts and focused tests were inspected alongside specs. Earlier status files are historical context, not absence/completion evidence. Existing later-module absence satisfies core independence only.
interpretation.evidenceLimits: All test/receipt references here are committed source or historical execution evidence. This inventory ran structural/source-coverage checks, not the whole test suite, physical qualification, legal review, cryptographic approval or live deployment.
interpretation.boundaries: Trading disabled; no production trust/key selection, live deployment/funds, paid services or external publication/messages.
interpretation.canonicalReferenceResolution: Each source.specRef resolves specifications[key].path (and its SHA256/sourceSections); section/line/unit/bullet/clause ordinals stay explicit. Each taskId resolves canonicalTasks[id] for owner, exclusiveFiles, reviewer, remainingAcceptance, dependencies, nextAction, implementationEvidence and separate qualification unless a source clause has a qualification override. Current partial implementation details/evidence also resolve specifications[key].sourceInspection. References factor the complete requirement record without duplicating execution or evidence.
interpretation.coverageRepair: Independent semantic review repaired four broad false-DONE mappings and adjacent G10/G11/G12/G16/G22/G25 browser/native-family obligations. Extraction now excludes only actual §1 Metadata, not Network metadata; substantive reference/dependency paragraphs remain explicit source clauses.

requirements.text: Validate a recoverable standalone basic trade on EVM and Solana, with all optional privacy/proof/map/courier/arbitration packages absent.
Tests use local/dev/test networks and fake fiat; no real payment or mainnet secrets enter automated tests.
TestCase record: `{id,requirement,chain,asset,wallet,browser,device,locale,routeMode,initialState,faults,steps,expectedAuthority,expectedUi,evidence}`.
Record exact wallet/browser/OS versions and device hardware at execution.
Target list includes Chromium/Firefox/WebKit automation plus physical Android and iPhone/iPad wallet handoff, keyboard, VoiceOver/TalkBack and 320px/400% zoom.
A support claim requires an actual passing combination; unsupported combinations are visible and cannot sign.

Journeys: onboard → backup/restore verification → wallet connect → create/discover/accept canonical terms → seller funds → finalized funding → exchange encrypted payment instructions → simulated buyer fiat payment → seller release before chain deadline → finalized receipt/export.
Separate journey: seller withholds, deadline passes, any caller triggers refund solely to seller.
Run native and each allowlisted ERC-20/SPL configuration independently.

Adversarial rows: wrong network/account, stale revision/quote, malicious amount/recipient, allowance mismatch, duplicate funding, token transfer failure, disallowed token extension, expiry-1/equality/+1, dropped/replaced/reorged/expired transaction, RPC split view, relay duplicates/offline, encrypted message tampering and unknown broadcast.
Restart at every journal transition; reconcile authoritative chain state before enabling another submission.
Use deterministic adapter fault injection for timing and protocol errors, plus real test-network/wallet integration for actual serialization/signature/handoff.
Capture sanitized event timeline, source/artifact hashes and chain transaction identifiers only in explicit test evidence.

Assert visible seller-withholding warning before buyer payment, no fiat-finality claim from chat/screenshot/proof, no optional-provider request in core-only build, and no direct connection when G05 strict routing is unsupported.
Cross-origin restore must create fresh G03 data keys while recovering records and pending intents.
A failed invariant, unexplained console/network secret leak, unresolved critical/high finding or untested mandatory wallet/chain is a release blocker.
TIMEOUT does not mean transaction failure; test reconciliation after delayed inclusion.
Automation cannot substitute for physical camera, deep-link, background eviction or assistive technology validation.
Fixtures must never teach production to bypass validation.
Evidence includes per-row results, testnet receipts, screenshots/accessibility observations, network capture showing route policy, crash checkpoints and independent reviewer signoff.
Repeat only affected rows after bounded changes, then complete the final core-only regression at the signed artifact.
No row is passed by this document; implementation, target execution and independent review remain pending.

Primary references (exact implementation revisions must be pinned in the evidence record): [Playwright browsers](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers); [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/); [EIP-1193](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1193).
Triage failures while keeping private trade content local by default and preserving existing escrow exits.
No analytics backend, automatic report upload or remote kill switch is required or introduced.
Maintainers cannot reverse basic escrow settlement or repair fiat loss; the runbook says so to users rather than implying otherwise.
In scope: severity classification, triage, containment through signed advisories, local redacted diagnostics, user export, and fund-recovery communication.
Out of scope: operating a support backend, collecting telemetry, and any claim that redaction is complete.
Applicability: no ZK circuit applies to G26.
No smart contract is introduced or modified by this specification.
It relies on the escrow exits fixed by G17/G18 and the deployment identities recorded under G25.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> detected
    detected --> triaged: severity assigned
    triaged --> contained: new funding disabled or endpoint removed
    contained --> recovering: recovery bundle published
    recovering --> reviewed: security reviewer signs off
    reviewed --> closed: postmortem changes filed
    contained --> recovering: containment failed, re-plan
```
IncidentRecord: `{incidentId, severity, reportedAt, affectedManifestDigests[], affectedDeploymentIds[], impact, hypothesis, containment, recovery, reviewer, status, advisoryDigest}`
- `status` is exactly one of `detected`, `triaged`, `contained`, `recovering`, `reviewed`, `closed`.
- `affectedManifestDigests` and `affectedDeploymentIds` use the digests from G25.
Free text does not replace them.
- `incidentId` is a random identifier.
It is not derived from a user, wallet or trade.
Local DiagnosticEvent allowlist (the only fields a diagnostic event may contain):
`{v, timeBucket, releaseId, module, errorCode, operation, routeState, chainNamespace, storageSchema}`
- `v` is the event format version.
- `timeBucket` is coarsened to the hour in UTC.
It is not an exact timestamp.
- `module`, `operation`, `routeState`, `chainNamespace` and `errorCode` take values from fixed enumerations in the typed error catalog (G13).
- `releaseId` and `storageSchema` are the values from the signed manifest in use.
Storage limits: at most 500 events or 1 MiB, whichever is reached first, retained for 7 days in local browser storage.
Older events and events beyond the cap are discarded.
Diagnostics are not a durable audit ledger.

Excluded from every diagnostic event, without exception: wallet and trade identifiers, escrow addresses, RPC query parameters, endpoint credentials, balances, bank details, chat content and evidence, key material and seeds, exact location, clipboard content, provider message bodies, stack traces and free-text error strings.
| Severity | Definition | Examples | Initial response |

| critical | Loss of funds, key compromise, or a defect that lets an attacker move escrowed funds | Signing key compromise; malicious release that alters settlement; escrow defect | Freeze new funding in an advisory immediately; open recovery package; notify security reviewer |

| high | Broad disclosure of user data, or a malicious endpoint or dependency served to users, without confirmed fund loss | Diagnostic leak; compromised RPC or relay endpoint returning altered data | Remove endpoint from future releases; advisory with affected hashes; notify reviewer |

| medium | Trade cannot complete through the normal path, funds are not at risk, a workaround exists | Gateway outage with a working origin; one module failing on one storage schema | Publish safe workaround; fix in next signed release |
| low | Cosmetic or single-user availability problem with an alternative route | Display fault; one locale string missing | Fix through normal release |
Classification rule: when in doubt between two levels, use the higher level and downgrade after triage.
Do not wait for perfect attribution before publishing a scoped advisory.
Triage starts from the report, not from the user's data.
The intake form asks only for:
Release identifier and manifest sequence, read from the app's about screen.
Module name, error code and operation, from the diagnostic preview.
Chain namespace (EVM or Solana) and storage schema.
Approximate UTC time of first occurrence.
Whether funds are at risk, answered yes, no or unsure.
Operators do not ask for, and do not record: seed phrases, private keys, passphrases, wallet addresses, trade IDs, amounts, bank details, chat messages, screenshots of trade screens, or receipts.
If a reporter sends any of these unprompted, the operator deletes the copy, does not quote it in the incident record, and replies with the rule above.
Support never requests a seed, private key or passphrase.
Triage steps:
Confirm severity from section 4.1 using the reported facts.
Record uncertainty as uncertainty.
Reproduce on a test network with the same `releaseId` where possible.
Decide whether the release, the endpoint or the origin is the affected component.
For critical or high incidents, move the incident to `triaged` and notify the security reviewer.
Containment, in order of preference:
Publish a new signed advisory release with a higher manifest `sequence` that disables new funding in the UI and removes any unsafe endpoint or dependency from the registry (G11).
Keep the existing escrow exits working.
On-chain settlement is immutable and cannot be paused by maintainers.
Publish the independent recovery bundle and the verified deployment identities (G25 section 4.6) at a static origin and on IPFS.
Do not remove or overwrite old artifacts.
Only a rollback to a previously reviewed source is allowed as a fix, and only with a higher sequence (G25 section 4.5).
Signing-key compromise requires an out-of-band trust re-bootstrap, not a same-origin unsigned replacement key.

The maintainers announce the new trust root on at least one channel that is independent of the compromised origin, and clients refuse manifests signed only by the old key after the announced cut-over sequence.
An advisory contains:
- affected manifest digests and deployment identifiers;
- observed facts, separated from hypotheses;
- stated uncertainty;
- safe recovery steps that work without the frontend;
- the signed publication sequence number and the advisory digest recorded in the IncidentRecord.
An advisory never contains user data, a claim that funds are safe when this is unverified, or an invented contact address.
- `collectDiagnostics()` returns only allowlisted fields from section 3.
It reads no raw error object.
- Error mapping drops provider message bodies and strips the query string and fragment from every URL before it is stored.
- Events are written to local storage only.
Nothing is sent automatically.
- `previewExport()` shows the exact final bytes as field-by-field rows and lists any warning, such as a field that was truncated to fit the cap.
- The user explicitly selects which events to include.
The export is capped at 1 MiB and downloaded to the user's device.
- Sharing the downloaded file is a separate action the user takes outside the app.
- `clearDiagnostics()` erases the local ring.
It works while the vault is locked and does not require the passphrase or any secret.
No redaction claim is made as mathematically complete.
The redaction is an allowlist, which is tested (section 7) and reviewed, not a proof.
Users are told the following, in plain language, through the verified channel only:
What is affected, in terms of release and network, without user-specific details.
That existing escrows settle on-chain and that the maintainers cannot reverse a completed settlement or repair fiat loss.
How to recover using the recovery bundle and section 4 of G25, with no frontend required.
How to confirm they are using the correct network and the expected code hash before signing.
That support will never ask for a seed phrase, private key or passphrase.
Templates must not promise a timeline, compensation or a specific outcome that the maintainers have not verified.
Security contact: instructions must name a real, maintained channel before any release.
If no such channel exists, the release is blocked.
No placeholder or invented address is published.
Diagnostics interface:
- `collectDiagnostics(): DiagnosticEvent[]` returns at most 500 allowlisted events.
- `previewExport(selection): { bytes: Uint8Array, rows: { field: string, value: string }[], warnings: string[] }` returns the final bytes shown to the user.
- `clearDiagnostics(): void` erases the local ring without unlocking the vault.
Error mapping: `mapError(raw): TypedError` keeps only the typed error code and the module.
It never copies `raw.message`, `raw.stack`, or any URL query or fragment.
Failure codes:
- `REDACTION_FAILED`: export is blocked.
Escrow recovery is not affected.
- `REPORT_TOO_LARGE`: the user must reduce the selection.
Nothing is uploaded.
Advisory interface: a signed JSON document carrying the fields in section 4.4, verified by the same trust root as the release manifest (G15).
- Browser storage can be evicted at any time.
Diagnostics may be lost; this is acceptable because they are not an audit record.
- Timing, module and error combinations can fingerprint a user even after redaction.
The export preview shows the combination so the user can decide.
- Malware or same-origin XSS can bypass diagnostics controls entirely.
The runbook does not claim otherwise.
- Clock rollback can distort `timeBucket`.
Buckets are advisory, not evidence.
- A social-engineering attacker may impersonate support.
The fixed rule that support never requests secrets is the control; users are told to verify the channel.
- Maintainers cannot reverse basic escrow settlement or repair fiat loss.
This is stated in every user-facing recovery message.
Tests and drills required before a release is accepted:

Inject known secret strings (seed-like values, a fake private key, a bank-like account number, a wallet address, a URL query token) into every raw error field, then assert none appear in the export bytes.
Locked-vault erase: lock the vault, call `clearDiagnostics()`, and confirm the ring is empty without a passphrase.
Capacity and age: write 501 events and events older than 7 days; confirm the cap and expiry.
Corrupt event storage: write invalid JSON and an out-of-range event to the ring; confirm both are discarded and the app still starts.
Clock rollback: move the clock backwards; confirm no crash and no negative age retention.
Offline advisory and recovery: confirm the recovery bundle and advisory load from the static origin and from IPFS with no network to the RPC.
`REDACTION_FAILED` and `REPORT_TOO_LARGE`: confirm export is blocked and escrow recovery still works.
Drill on test networks, separately: bad release, compromised endpoint, signing-key incident and lost origin.
Record recovery evidence and postmortem changes without personal data.
Each drill is recorded with the exact revisions tested.
Operational ownership, implementation and independent rehearsal remain pending.
No drill in this document has been performed.

Primary references (exact implementation revisions must be pinned in the evidence record): [OWASP logging guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html); [NIST incident response](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final).

Offer creation, discover/match, counterpart verification, wallet connect, chain/network confirmation, quote expiration, escrow funding, payment-instructions exchange, evidence presentation, settlement attestation, dispute/timeout, release/refund, receipt/export, recovery after tab/device loss.
Define actors, state transitions, deadline, fees, custody, recovery, accessibility and test case for each.
No fiat transfer or payment-processor settlement should be claimed final solely from a screenshot, unverified webhook or zkTLS proof.

requirements.text: Encode selected public shareable data locally and require explicit review before use.
QR contents are hostile input; scanning is never navigation, wallet connection, signature or import authorization.
Secrets, mnemonics, decrypted evidence and authentication tokens are excluded from generic sharing.
Envelope v1: `{protocol:"p2p-offramp-qr",v:1,type,requestId,createdAt,expiresAt,chain,originHint,payload,payloadSha256,signature?}`.

Allowed types: public-address, trade-invite, payment-request, release-fingerprint and recovery-fingerprint. requestId is 16 random bytes hex; timestamps are UTC seconds integers, default invite validity 10 minutes and maximum 24 hours; hashes are SHA-256 canonical RFC 8785 payload bytes. chain is required for address/payment/trade. originHint is display-only, never trust.
Signature, when present, uses the type-specific accepted identity profile (not automatically release signing keys); unsigned payloads remain explicitly unauthenticated.
Generate/scan locally using a pinned reviewed library; no remote QR image service.
A single code is at most 2,048 UTF-8 envelope bytes with no compression, scripts or embedded image data.
Oversized payloads use a downloadable file plus local hash fingerprint; animated multi-frame backup transport is deferred/unsupported until independently specified.
Encrypted G03 backups use file transport, explicit sensitive-ciphertext confirmation and ordinary recovery checks; a public hash is not an off-device download capability.
Scanner decodes at most one candidate per user confirmation, then parses strict schema with depth 8 and 64 KiB file-import ceiling for public envelopes.
Reject unknown fields/version/type, invalid Unicode, oversized content, stale invites and chain mismatch.
Show full recipient, amount/base units, chain, expiry, identity/signature state and permissions before accept.

`decodeQr(bytes)` returns a validated candidate only; `reviewCandidate(candidate,context)` produces explicit confirmation UI; `commitImport` merges through authoritative domain rules and cannot overwrite live funded terms.
Local request-ID deduplication prevents accidental repeated import but is not global anti-replay security.
A trade invite must fetch/revalidate signed current terms through G05 before funding.
Wallet-session QR uses its connector's protocol/parser and is explicitly sensitive; generic public QR sharing never copies session URIs.
Every QR has copy/paste/file/manual fallback; camera starts on user gesture and stops tracks on accept/cancel/background.
QR_TOO_LARGE, TYPE_UNSUPPORTED, HASH_MISMATCH, EXPIRED, CHAIN_MISMATCH and IMPORT_CONFLICT leave storage/transactions unchanged.
URLs render as text; only separately approved allowlisted links can open.
A matching hash detects accidental change but authenticates no sender.
Camera denial and same-device scanning use file/paste fallback.
Clipboard poisoning, QR replacement, phishing and screenshot persistence remain user-visible risks.
Roundtrip each type on physical iOS/Android/desktop with printed, low-light, inverted and partial codes.

ENCRYPTION_REQUIRED rejects private persistence without unlocked vault; LOCAL_LIMIT_REACHED offers wait/cancel without deleting state; PORTAL_READ_ONLY explains external recovery instructions.
Same-origin malicious script can read unlocked data; local challenges cannot stop bots or network abuse.
Download hashes only help when obtained from trusted independent distribution.
Private data never enters permanent static/IPFS releases.

requirements.text: Model an observer that controls or monitors the trader's access network but cannot break properly authenticated TLS or compromise endpoints.
The goal is bounded disclosure and honest routing labels, not guaranteed anonymity against global correlation.
| Observer sees or controls | App protection | Remaining exposure |
| Destination IP, packet sizes and timing | G05 enforced private route where supported | First hop and traffic correlation remain |
| DNS queries | Route-specific resolver configuration and tests | Browser/OS/extension lookups may be outside app control |
| HTTP content without TLS | HTTPS/WSS-only endpoint registry | Malicious endpoint still sees application data |
| Connection failure or censorship | Bounded failure with explicit status | Availability cannot be guaranteed |
| Wallet-extension traffic | Independent routing evidence | Unknown wallet coverage blocks strict signing |
RPC, relays, maps, update checks, proof services and wallet traffic are separate channels.
A Tor browser session does not prove a wallet extension's traffic follows the same route.
Before opening a network connection, the broker must evaluate channel, endpoint and current generation under G05.
Ordinary direct mode requires a visible direct-connection label.
Strict mode requires verified private coverage per channel.
Mixed direct/private traffic cannot receive an aggregate protected badge.
A route failure invalidates permits and closes sockets; never retry directly.
Do not send diagnostics, connectivity probes, external fonts, avatars, or explorer previews outside policy.
A privacy-mode change takes effect for future I/O and cannot hide earlier traffic.
The client does not implement packet padding or global traffic mixing in v1 and MUST NOT claim resistance to a global timing observer.
No new cryptographic primitive or ZK circuit is defined in this threat model.
Use the G05 `RouteEvidence` and `TransportPolicy` interfaces.
UI state is a projection of actual broker evidence: `direct`, `verified-private`, `unknown`, `unsupported`.
Persist user preferences only; evidence and permits are recreated every session.
Endpoint health checks are ordinary policy-authorized reads and cannot bootstrap trust in a routing path merely by succeeding.
Fixed error codes distinguish policy refusal from remote timeout without recording destination paths or payloads.
Network MITM may replace unprotected downloads or downgrade HTTP: reject insecure endpoint schemes and verify versioned release artifacts.
A valid TLS certificate authenticates an endpoint, not its honesty.
Private routing shifts trust to route infrastructure and may reveal the destination to the exit or service.
No UI may present a VPN/Tor checkbox as a proof that browser, wallet, DNS, OS, and all extensions are hidden.
Capture browser and test-device network traffic for ordinary mode, strict mode, private-route outage, reconnect, page load and wallet signing.
Test DNS and wallet traffic separately and record the capture boundary; a page-only trace is insufficient to prove OS-wide coverage.
Spy tests assert zero direct requests after strict-route loss.
Simulate captive portal, TLS failure, redirect and endpoint censorship.
Expected result is refusal or explicit degraded state, never hidden fallback.

| Adversary condition | Core response | Limit |
| Brief access to locked device/browser | Encrypted local vault, no auto-unlock | Weak passphrase/offline copies remain vulnerable |
| Access while app unlocked | Page-hide and idle locking, minimized rendered data | Screen capture and plaintext memory may already be exposed |

| Copied backup/storage | G02/G03 authenticated encryption | Cannot retract copies or guarantee erasure |

Lock invokes G01/G02 synchronously and removes sensitive UI state; asynchronous work checks session generation before returning plaintext.
Page hide and five-minute idle lock follow G02 exactly.
A crash/restart begins locked.
Show only the information needed for the current flow; hide chat/payment details behind explicit reveal controls after unlock.
User-controlled export includes an explicit local disclosure action.
Locking does not delete vaults, change chain positions, or rotate counterpart identities.
Refund/release deadlines continue on-chain while the app is locked.

Do not market memory overwrite or IndexedDB deletion as forensic erasure.

Confirm locking generates no chain transaction, deletion, network beacon or identity rotation.

Core basic escrow has no payment oracle, upgrade authority, juror or automatic fiat-finality claim; optional variants require separate opted-in deployments.
Assets: escrowed token balances, correct buyer/seller identity, release authorization, dispute state, trade commitments, client-side credentials, private messages and payment confidentiality.

- `escrowBalance >= sum(outstanding liabilities)` for tracked tokens under supported token semantics, with clear handling of unsolicited transfers.
- For each trade, `releasedAmount + refundedAmount <= depositedAmount`; only one terminal disposition, including dispute paths.
- Funds leave escrow only after authorized, fresh settlement conditions or a separately defined timelock/dispute transition.
- Signature message is domain-separated by chain, verifying contract, action, trade ID, amount, token, payer, recipient, nonce and deadline.
Each authorization can be consumed at most once.
- A contested fiat payment is not final merely because a browser screenshot or TLS proof says a transfer was initiated.
Settlement semantics must be separately defined.
- Transaction ordering, gas price, block timestamps and third-party token behavior may be adversarial.
Unsafe (demonstration only):
Safer foundation, assuming the contract has precisely defined token and trade accounting; import audited library versions and tailor permissions:
**Required beyond example:** safe deposit flow, role/dispute authorization, all cross-function locks, fee-token policy, state invariant checks and event design.
Library import path depends on pinned OpenZeppelin major version.
EIP-712 domain `D=(name,version,chainId,verifyingContract)`; digest `H=keccak256(0x1901 || domainSeparator(D) || hashStruct(action))`.
Struct fields must include `tradeId,token,amount,buyer,seller,recipient,nonce,deadline,action`.
Verify `ecrecover(H,signature)` via audited ECDSA recovery enforcing `0 < s <= n/2`, valid `r`, supported recovery id, nonzero signatory and exact intended signer.
EIP-712 provides structural binding, not automatic replay protection.
Use `usedNonces[signer][nonce]` or action-scoped bitmaps; atomically consume nonce before any external call; expiration must be checked on-chain.
Preferred for manually negotiated P2P exchange: immutable signed quote with explicit base units and expiry; do not fetch a DEX spot price to determine contractual entitlement.

For automated conversion, require feed allowlists, maximum age `block.timestamp - updatedAt <= maxAge`, circuit breakers, deviation `abs(P_new-P_reference)/P_reference <= delta`, appropriate decimals and a protocol-defined fallback that never silently releases at an attacker-selected rate.
TWAP resists instantaneous price manipulation but does not eliminate long-window manipulation or broken markets.
Simulate flash-loan adversaries manipulating liquidity and collateral.
If there is **no swap**, a sandwich-style swap attack is not directly applicable to an escrow transfer, but order-dependent release, offer fills, and cancellation races remain.
Bind `recipient`, `maxAmount`, `minReceived` (where relevant), `deadline`, `nonce` and escrow ID to consent.
Build a terminal state machine so `release` and `refund` cannot both succeed.
Private transaction submission may reduce public mempool exposure but entails relayer trust and offers no absolute MEV protection.
For core v1, G11 immutable deployment policy supersedes broad discussion of timelocked/proxy alternatives.
A proof or payment-gateway response is evidence only, never core release authority.
G12 durable reservation and chain-specific reconciliation supersede generic resubmit-on-error suggestions.
Severity is a prioritization label, not a numeric probability or proof of exploitability.
Address rendering: contract address originates from signed deployment manifest, not payment-message text.
On confirmation show checksummed complete address, chain, token, decimals, amount and chain explorer canonical origin.
Disable submit on wallet chain mismatch; detect recent clipboard paste but do not silently replace it.
Browser checksums detect mistakes, not malicious but correctly checksummed addresses.

RPC policy: query `eth_chainId`, `eth_getBlockByNumber` for agreed finalized height/hash, `eth_getCode` for deployed escrow, `eth_getLogs` with canonical block hashes, and `eth_getTransactionReceipt`.
Compare two independently controlled provider endpoints (three if possible); transport diversity alone does not guarantee independence.
If providers disagree on finalized block hash or required state, stop settlement UX and give manual chain-explorer verification.
Verify receipt is on canonical chain and has required contract/address/topics, then wait chain-specific finality.

Avoid trusting `eth_call` output alone; where supported use EIP-1186 state proofs and verify against trusted block headers, recognizing that full light-client consensus verification is a separate substantial subsystem.
A two-RPC majority is **not** cryptographic consensus.
Wallet: EIP-1193 `accountsChanged` and `chainChanged` events invalidate cached simulation, signature requests and session assumptions.
Confirm typed-data text and domain in independent UI; allow safe cancellation.
A compromised wallet extension can defeat page checks; do not promise protection against malicious signing UI.
Payment evidence: an authenticated TLS transcript may establish what a server returned at a point in time, not that funds are irrevocably transferred.
Trust assumptions include verifier implementation, certificate chain, attestor/notary honesty, freshness and provenance of the returned data.
Release policy requires rail-specific finality, proof audience, amount/currency, destination/payee consistency and dispute controls.
Every enabled-capability attack row maps to a test fixture and evidence before release.
`not-applicable` requires a concrete scope reason (e.g. arbitration not installed), never a blanket waiver.
Findings use sanitized local IDs and fixed descriptions, not secrets, bank data or private witnesses.
An unresolved critical/high finding blocks the affected enabled capability.
Failed/erroring tests are not mitigation evidence.
| ID | Attack / entry point | Failure mode | Defenses and verification |

| C-01 Critical | Classic reentrancy in escrow refund/release | External token or callback reenters before liability changes | CEI + nonReentrant + zero terminal state before transfer; malicious callback fuzz |
| C-02 Critical | Cross-function reentrancy | Refund path reaches release/cancel under shared accounting | Shared lock and mutually exclusive state machine; invariant across all entrypoints |

| C-03 High | Read-only reentrancy | Callback sees transient price/balance state and triggers downstream decision | Snapshot finalized state, avoid price functions depending on temporarily inconsistent external balances |

| C-04 Critical | Signature replay/malleability | Reused or alternate signatures authorize unintended releases | EIP-712 domain; low-s ECDSA, strict v, reject zero signer, per-action nonce/bitmap and expiry |
| C-05 Critical | Chain/contract replay | Signature valid on fork, proxy or other deployment | `chainId`, verifyingContract, immutable domain version and deployment mapping |

| C-06 Critical | Arbitrary ERC20 callback / fee-on-transfer | Incorrect credited escrow amount or malicious token transfer hook | Whitelist known semantics; checked balance delta when supported; SafeERC20; reject unsupported rebasing/fee tokens |

| C-07 High | Oracle manipulation / flash loan | Single-block DEX price used as settlement rate or collateral threshold | Avoid oracle if fixed price; otherwise curated feeds, heartbeat, staleness/deviation checks, TWAP and economic circuit breakers |

| C-08 High | MEV/front-running/reorder | Release/refund parameters or offers copied/reordered | Full parameter binding in signatures, commit-reveal when appropriate, short expiries, nonce, slippage/minOut where swap exists |
| C-09 Critical | Arbitrary external calls | Attacker chooses target, delegatecall or calldata | No generic privileged `call`/delegatecall; explicit target allowlist, audit adapters |
| C-10 High | Role/upgrade compromise | Proxy/admin drains escrow or changes release logic | Prefer immutable contracts; timelocked limited upgrades, multisig, governance scope tests |
| C-11 High | Denial of service | Reverting receiver/gas grief stalls pooled settlements | Pull-payment accounting, isolate each trade, bounded iterations and retry paths |
| C-12 High | Arithmetic/rounding | Decimal truncation/overflow misallocates transfers | Solidity >=0.8 checked arithmetic, token decimal rules, no unchecked casts, dust invariants |
| C-13 High | Time and liveness | Timestamp drift permits premature action / frozen funds | Explicit bounded windows, monotonic state transitions, escape hatches and dispute liveness proof |

| C-14 High | Transaction simulation mismatch | Client simulates different pending/final state than execution | Simulate exact call at current block; revalidate allowance/account/chain just before send |

| C-15 Critical | UI/clipboard address replacement | Victim sends tokens to poisoned/clipboard-spoofed address | Address derived from verified escrow contract, prominent full-address confirmation, QR and checksum, wallet simulation |

| C-16 Critical | Provider injection or phishing | Malicious `window.ethereum` alters account, chain, signature presentation | Explicit wallet selection, EIP-1193 event monitoring, local typed-data preview; warn that compromised provider can still deceive |

| C-17 High | RPC tampering/equivocation | Fake deposit, malicious chain ID, falsified receipts/balances | Pin chain/genesis and contract code hash; compare independent providers at same finalized block; fail closed on split |
| C-18 High | Network MITM | RPC or app JS swapped | HTTPS authenticated transport, CSP/SRI/content manifest, signature verify; on-chain proofs when possible |

| C-19 Critical | Proof forged/replayed | Reuse of payment proof for unrelated trade or stale bank activity | Bind cryptographic proof to trade, amount, currency, payee, proof issuance/expiry, issuer and audience; nonce consumed once |

| C-20 High | Payment reversal/fraud | "Paid" bank page later reverses or account holder disputes | Explicit bank/rail settlement-finality policy, separate dispute window, human arbitration or approved reversible-risk model |
| C-21 High | Messaging replay/Sybil | Fake counterpart or replayed release confirmation | End-to-end peer authentication, signed trade context, expiration, replay database and rate controls |
| C-22 High | Privacy linkage | Public chain/relay/fiat metadata reveals identity | Per-trade keys, envelope padding, avoid shared address reuse, clear traffic correlation risk |
| C-23 High | Secret leakage via browser state | XSS/extension/storage exposes signer key | External wallet, memory confinement, encrypted local records, strict CSP, key lifecycle tests |
| C-24 High | Chain reorg/bridge risk | Receipt counted before finality, bridged asset depegs | Chain-specific finality threshold, canonical block tracking, bridge allowlist or exclusion |
| C-25 High | Batch partial execution | Successful payout mixed with failed transfer creates ambiguous liabilities | Atomic per-trade transitions or explicit recoverable partial state machine |
| C-26 High | Permit misuse | Unbounded approvals and forged permit domain | Token-scoped allowances, spender confirmation, permit nonce/chain binding, revocation UX |
| C-27 High | Fake token and decimal confusion | Impersonated stablecoin or incorrect units | Exact chain + token address + code/issuer identity allowlists; integer base units throughout |
| C-28 High | Relayer censorship or bribery | P2P/chain action never appears | Relay diversity, retransmission bounds, direct-chain emergency action and deterministic expiry |
| C-29 High | Frontend dependency supply chain | Compromised npm/CDN package exfiltrates wallet trade state | Lockfile, SRI/manifest, signed releases, SBOM, least privilege, no runtime dependencies |
| C-30 Medium | Side-channel metadata | Relay ciphertext length and timing reveal trade state | Class-based padding, trade-id rotation, optional delayed batching, quantified residual leakage |

Echidna on invariants, Slither on source, differential tests against reference implementations, independent audit before live funds.
Model-check permissions and liveness if formal tooling is available.

Map [NCSC Common Cyber Attacks](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/white-papers/common-cyber-attacks-reducing-impact) to this project: phishing -> fake wallet/escrow origin tests; malware -> compromised-browser/extension risk and hardware-wallet confirmations; missing patches -> lockfile/CI vulnerability gates; insecure configuration -> CSP/permission-policy tests; excessive privilege -> least-privileged CI and no contract admin superuser; missing monitoring -> privacy-preserving signed release and on-chain anomaly signals; poor incident response -> public vulnerability disclosure and emergency pause/recovery criteria.
These controls reduce exposure but cannot eliminate malicious endpoint risks.

The [NCSC Secure communications principles](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/sites/default/files/pdfs/publication/secure-communication-principles.pdf) add communication-layer cases: sender impersonation, unauthorized relay-node plaintext access, compromised key infrastructure, audit-data exfiltration, abusive admin roles, metadata aggregation and relay monoculture.

Apply [CPA Build Standard v1.4](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/files/CPA-Build_Standard_1-4.pdf) as a build-assurance evidence checklist, **not a certification claim**: signed threat-model revision; independent review of contract release state machine; static-analysis report; property-test seeds; fuzz corpus; third-party dependency/compilation manifest; repeatable release artifact; vulnerability intake/triage; rollback and emergency recovery exercise.

Archive PoCs are untrusted and must be manually reviewed before isolated reproduction; never deploy them into escrow clients. [Packet Storm API guidance](https://www.packetstatic.com/help/view/1) indicates credentials and access conditions, so avoid embedding a feed key in a static client.

Bind each optional proof to exactly one application statement, trade, chain, verifier and action.
Public inputs are not encrypted; exclude bank account numbers, names, raw transcripts and secrets.
This contract precedes any circuit implementation.

Application envelope: `{v:1,app:"p2p-offramp",statementId,circuitId,circuitVersion,vkHash,chainNamespace,chainReference,deploymentId,tradeId,termsHash,action,policyHash,issuedAt,expiresAt,challenge,claimCommitment,nullifier}`.
Hashes and challenge are 32-byte lowercase hex; timestamps are UTC integer seconds encoded as decimal strings; chain and deployment identifiers use the chain registry.
No floating-point amounts.
A statement-specific schema declares amount/currency/time fields, byte bounds and private witness layout.
Nullifier scope and unlinkability analysis are mandatory per statement; a global identity-derived nullifier is prohibited by default.
Reject unknown/duplicate fields and oversized envelope before canonicalization.
Encode RFC 8785 canonical JSON with all amounts and timestamps as validated canonical decimal strings.
Compute domain digest SHA-256 over UTF-8 `p2p-offramp/proof-input/v1 ` followed by canonical envelope bytes excluding proof bytes.
A reviewed circuit adapter must constrain this digest to the full witness-derived statement, not accept it as an unconstrained public label.
Field conversion is versioned: each 32-byte digest becomes two big-endian unsigned 128-bit limbs in order, never modulo-reduced.
The selected circuit must prove range constraints for limbs and bind all fields; circuit admission records list the exact ordered public vector.
Challenge is 32 random bytes from the verifier session, scoped to trade/action, expires in at most 10 minutes and is consumed once after successful acceptance.
`encodePublicInputs(envelope,statementSchema)` returns canonical bytes, digest and ordered field vector.

`verifyBoundProof(proof,envelope,expectedContext)` compares every expected chain/deployment/trade/action/policy field before expensive verification, then checks circuit allowlist and nullifier/challenge state.
Proofs are at most 16 MiB and run off the UI thread; tighter statement-specific limits override.
Persist accepted claim digest and verifier version, not witness data.
PROOF_CONTEXT_MISMATCH, NONCANONICAL_INPUT, PUBLIC_INPUT_RANGE, CHALLENGE_EXPIRED, PROOF_REPLAY and VERIFIER_UNSUPPORTED reject without updating accepted state.
Wall-clock expiry is an evidence UI policy, never a chain deadline authority.
A proof replayed on another origin/trade/chain cannot satisfy a fresh challenge; exported proof receipts remain publicly linkable.
Locally consumed challenges cannot provide global replay protection across independent verifiers.
Golden byte/limb vectors include empty/maximum strings, reordered JSON, Unicode, leading-zero decimal rejection and both 128-bit limbs at bounds.
Mutate every public field while retaining the same proof and require rejection.
Circuit review must demonstrate no unconstrained public digest or witness field.
Concurrent acceptance tests require one local state commit; global uniqueness requires a separately specified on-chain nullifier registry.

PROOF_UNSUPPORTED is normal, not a reason to downgrade to screenshot verification or upload secrets.

G06 provenance and G05 routing apply to artifact/provider fetches.

Independently verify proofs and invalid-proof rejection using the pinned verifier.

Keep spending, messaging, vault, backup and optional stealth capabilities cryptographically separate.
External wallets retain spending authority: the client MUST NOT derive wallet spending keys from a login signature, password, Nostr secret or recovery export.
This specification defines derivation context and ownership, not a new stealth construction.

A KeyPurpose record is `{v:1,purpose:"messaging"|"vault"|"backup"|"stealth-view"|"stealth-spend",generationId,createdAt,implementationId}`. generationId is a fresh 128-bit random identifier, never a user identifier.
The vault owns a fresh random 256-bit AES key; encrypted backup/recovery follows G02/G03.
A messaging secret is independently generated and encrypted in the vault.
Stealth capability owns separately generated scheme-valid scalars through its reviewed adapter.
Purpose metadata is authenticated, not a way to convert one key into another.
A nonextractable CryptoKey does not protect against hostile same-origin script invoking it.
Generate entropy using crypto.getRandomValues; abort on failure.
Do not use Math.random, timestamps, wallet addresses or low-entropy phrases.

Where an adapter explicitly requires derivation from an existing high-entropy root, use HKDF-SHA-256 with separately random 32-byte salt and UTF-8 info `p2p-offramp/key/v1/<purpose>/<adapterId>/<generationId>`; each purpose/adapter has its own allowlisted info and output size.
This HKDF rule is NOT a replacement for G02's fixed password wrapping: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256, 600,000 iterations, AES-256-GCM.
Curve scalar conversion MUST use the selected protocol's specified rejection/reduction algorithm and test vectors, never an unreviewed modulo shortcut.
G03 restoration decrypts the old archive, creates a fresh vault data key and generation, then re-encrypts records atomically; it does not reuse archive encryption keys for writes.
`createPurposeKey(purpose, adapterId)` returns an opaque capability or typed unsupported result; raw bytes never reach UI reducers.
`rotateMessagingKey()` creates a new identity and warns that existing conversations need explicit reauthentication.
`destroySession()` drops all key references and worker state; best-effort buffer overwrite is not guaranteed browser memory erasure.
Export includes only G03-authorized encrypted key records; no spending-wallet secrets.
Reject unknown purpose, reused generation ID, missing secure context and unsupported primitive with KEY_PURPOSE_INVALID, KEY_GENERATION_FAILED or CRYPTO_UNSUPPORTED.
Fail before persistent mutation.
Domain separation does not provide forward secrecy, protect weak backup passwords, or undo root compromise.
Cross-purpose substitution and accidental log/export disclosure are explicit threats.
Rotation must preserve old encrypted records until migration and recovery checks succeed.
Known-answer HKDF vectors plus application info-byte vectors must verify differing purpose/adapter/generation changes output.
Test entropy failure, locked-vault calls, wrong AAD, archive restore with fresh-key assertion and rotation interrupted before commit.
Review key-flow diagrams for any path from app keys to wallet spending authority.
Browser interoperability and independent cryptographic review remain release gates.

M2 basic escrow continues to use a directly bound recipient.
Stealth applies only to new trade terms that explicitly select a supported scheme and deployment.

The external wallet must support the eventual recipient's spending/recovery workflow; ordinary wallet connect does not imply stealth support.

1. **crypto-adapter** holds ephemeral secrets in purpose-scoped worker/operation handles.
It exposes protocol-specific public results, never a generic raw-key getter to UI.
Use `crypto.getRandomValues` and selected reviewed protocol libraries; random-source failure is fatal.
G01/G02 govern messaging and vault keys; wallet spending seeds never enter app JS.
2. **wallet-adapter** applies EIP-1193 request semantics, EIP-712 domain separation with `chainId`, `verifyingContract`, version, action-specific nonce and deadline.
Re-read wallet chain/account immediately before submission.
Provider is not a data-integrity oracle.
3. **escrow-adapter** pins ABI, chain ID, deployment address and runtime bytecode/code hash per release manifest.
Read via at least two independently operated RPCs for important finalized states and compare block hash/state; unresolved disagreement stops release, not majority-vote blind signing.

4. **message-adapter** implements `encodeEncryptedEnvelope -> pad -> transport.send` and reverse receive path; authentication, replay window, expiration and envelope version are independent of Nostr/Waku.
Do not send keys, fiat credentials, raw bank information, or plaintext proofs to relays.
5. **proof-adapter** implements `verifyProof(proof, expectedPolicy, freshness, audience, tradeId)`.
Bind statement to trade ID, amount, currency, payee commitment, proof expiry, issuer/attestor key and verifier version.
An attestation about a webpage is **not** intrinsically irreversible bank settlement.
6. **storage-adapter** uses G02 exact bounded snapshot encryption and authenticated metadata, G03 fresh-key recovery and G09 migrations.
No per-record alternate format or mnemonic/spending-seed import is authorized in core.
7. **routing-adapter** checks whether a privacy transport is actually active.
A normal browser fetch cannot be labeled "Tor" simply because a JS package exists.
Failure should be clearly surfaced, with a no-network or explicitly consented fallback.
AES-256-GCM encryption: `(C,T) = AEAD_Encrypt(K, IV, P, AAD)`, with independent unpredictable 96-bit nonce per encryption under a key.
HKDF: `PRK=HMAC_SHA256(salt,IKM)`; `K=HKDF_Expand(PRK,"p2p-offramp/v1/" || purpose || context,32)`.

Argon2id: `K=Argon2id(password, randomPersistentSalt, m,t,p,32)`, parameters calibrated on supported low-end devices and re-evaluated periodically. **A salt cannot be ephemeral if the encrypted vault needs later recovery**; store the salt alongside ciphertext.
For transient-only records, use a random session key and erase it on session teardown.
Candidate rows are options to evaluate, not simultaneously enabled dependencies.
Argon2id, BIP39/BIP32 and generic HTML sanitization do not override the core G02 profile, no-wallet-seed policy or G04 text-only rendering.
Choosing an SDK requires a G06 inventory entry with exact version/integrity, source, license and executed independent vectors.

This project adopts the latter as an evidence-driven build process, **not** a claim of CPA certification.

Implement them as a seven-column scorecard for Nostr/Waku/XMTP/TLS attestors, distinguishing relay operators from cryptographic endpoints.

Manifest v1: `{format:"p2p-offramp-release",version:1,channel,sequence,releaseId,sourceCommit,buildRecipeDigest,lockfileDigest,sbomDigest,createdAt,expiresAt,minStorageSchema,maxStorageSchema,assets,deployments,predecessorDigest}`. sequence is an integer 1..2^53-1; created/expires are UTC seconds integers; expiry is at most 30 days from creation. assets is sorted by normalized relative path and each item is `{path,bytes,sha256}`; no absolute paths, dot segments, symlinks, duplicate/case-colliding paths or query strings.
Limits: 10,000 assets, 256 MiB total bundle, 1 MiB manifest. deployments bind chain identity, contract/program address, code digest and immutable/upgrade authority facts.
Personal data, credentials, private RPC tokens and trade artifacts are prohibited.
Release signatures use ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 through WebCrypto, 64-byte IEEE-P1363 big-endian r||s signatures encoded unpadded base64url (not ASN.1 DER).
Public keys are JWK `{kty:"EC",crv:"P-256",x,y,key_ops:["verify"],ext:true}` with exactly 32-byte coordinates.
No private key appears in client assets or build environment.
RFC 8785 canonical UTF-8 manifest bytes, excluding the detached signature envelope, are prefixed with `p2p-offramp/release/v1\n` and signed.
Reject unknown algorithms, malformed lengths, duplicate fields and noncanonical representations.
The keyId is SHA-256 of canonical `{crv,kty,x,y}`; trust comes from an independently verified key fingerprint, not from a key delivered beside an untrusted signature.
First hash final assets, then construct/sign manifest, then package manifest/signature beside assets.
A distribution CID is external because embedding a directory's own CID would be circular.
A signed ReleaseLocator binds manifest digest to CID/package digest in a second domain `p2p-offramp/release-locator/v1\n`; locator uses the same key/signature encoding.

Its canonical signed payload is `{v:1,channel,sequence,manifestSha256,cid,archiveSha256,createdAt,expiresAt}`; channel/sequence/timestamps must exactly match the manifest, CID must parse as CIDv1, and archiveSha256 covers the optional downloadable archive (null when absent).
A locator envelope `{keyId,alg:"ES256-P1363",signature}` is detached from that payload.
The textual `\n` in signature domain descriptions denotes one byte 0x0a, not backslash plus n.
Require signature r and s in the valid P-256 scalar range; do not use signature bytes as release identity, because ECDSA signature representations can be malleable.
Release identity is the signed manifest digest.
Verify manifest signature, asset path set, byte lengths and hashes before treating a downloaded package as authenticated.
No unlisted executable asset is permitted.
Detached envelope: `{v:1,keyId,alg:"ES256-P1363",manifestSha256,signature}`.
`verifyRelease(bytes,envelope,trustedKeys,highestSequence)` returns verified metadata or a typed rejection; verification never imports a supplied public key as trusted.
Historical releases retain immutable identifiers.
Rotation requires a signed trust transition from an already trusted key plus out-of-band announcement; suspected key compromise requires independent re-bootstrap.
SIGNATURE_INVALID, KEY_UNTRUSTED, MANIFEST_EXPIRED, RELEASE_ROLLBACK, ASSET_MISMATCH and MANIFEST_UNSUPPORTED fail closed for installation.
Existing recovery documentation remains available.
Locally stored maximum sequence helps only on that origin/profile; fresh origins, cleared storage and wrong device clocks weaken rollback/expiry checks.
A hostile host can replace both verifier JavaScript and embedded public keys: browser self-checks alone do not authenticate the initial application.

Specify economic and authorization properties for immutable basic escrow; proofs do not prove fiat receipt, user honesty, browser safety or network liveness.
EVM and Solana models must refine the same economic state machine through chain-specific transition rules.
Model state per escrow: `{seller,buyer,asset,principal,deadline,termsHash,status}` where status is Unfunded, Funded, Released or Refunded.
Participants, asset, principal, deadline and terms hash are immutable after funding.
Principal is a positive bounded base-unit integer, never floating point.
Allowed assets exclude unsupported transfer behavior.
Chain time, not local UI time, selects deadline guards.
Fees, if introduced, must be explicit immutable terms and separately conserved; the initial basic model assumes no protocol fee.

Transitions: fund by seller transfers exactly principal into custody and sets Funded; release requires seller authority and chainTime < deadline and pays the bound buyer; refund requires chainTime >= deadline and pays the seller, with any caller permitted to trigger it.
Terminal states cannot transition.

Invariants: escrow liability equals principal only while Funded; payouts to buyer+seller never exceed deposited principal; exactly one terminal payout; no participant substitution; no caller-controlled payout destination; external calls cannot observe a still-spendable liability after settlement.
Donation balances are not escrow principal.
For EVM, model revert atomicity and checks-effects-interactions/reentrancy guards.
For Solana, model atomic instructions, signer/owner constraints, PDA derivation and valid token/mint ownership explicitly.
Each property record is `{id,plainStatement,formalStatement,modelCommit,implementationFunction,assumptions,toolVersion,result,counterexampleDigest}`.
Prove safety under arbitrary authorized/unauthorized call ordering and include transition refinement obligations.
Liveness is conditional: if valid refund/release can be submitted, funded by gas and eventually included before relevant guards, it can settle.
No proof may claim timely inclusion, fiat recovery, or seller cooperation.
Token behavior and chain-time assumptions must match the allowlist and deployed chain.
PROOF_UNKNOWN, MODEL_IMPLEMENTATION_GAP or COUNTEREXAMPLE_FOUND blocks the affected property gate.
Solver timeout is unknown, not proved.
Unbounded loops, arithmetic overflow, account aliasing and malicious token hooks must be addressed in the real implementation model or explicitly excluded by enforced validation.
Separate program correctness from trusted compiler/runtime assumptions.
Provide executable boundary tests at deadline-1, deadline and deadline+1, adversarial call sequences, randomized amounts, repeated settlements and failed transfers.
Review every model assumption against implementation checks; link counterexamples to regression tests.
Independent proof/model review and chain-specific deployment validation are required before claiming coverage.
Basic escrow always retains explicit dishonest-seller withholding risk.

CID changes, gateway changes and GitHub Pages deployment paths have distinct isolation effects; never infer vault absence means the user's keys or funds do not exist.
Bootstrap trust through a previously authenticated distribution key fingerprint and independently checked archive/verifier.
A first visit to a hostile gateway cannot authenticate itself by running its own checker.
Discovery fetches obey G05 route policy and have 1 MiB manifest/30-second request bounds.
Verify signature, expiry, channel, deployment identities and monotonically increasing release sequence against local accepted state.
Show current/candidate fingerprints, schema compatibility, recovery requirement and known changes.
Ask the user to export/verify G03 backup before opening a new origin.
Restore creates fresh G03 vault keys and reconciles authoritative chain state; no transaction replay.
New release starts locked and with wallet disconnected.
Updates while a wallet signature request is pending wait until that request is cancelled/resolved.
`checkForUpdate()` returns none, candidate, untrusted, stale or unreachable; unavailable discovery leaves the installed client readable with explicit stale status.
`acceptUpdate(candidate)` writes verified sequence to current-origin storage and opens a user-confirmed destination, never transfers plaintext secrets through URLs, postMessage or clipboard.
Key rotation uses an old-key-signed transition plus independent publication; compromise requires manual trust re-bootstrap.
No service worker is required; if introduced, its cache/version/eviction lifecycle needs separate review.
ORIGIN_UNSUPPORTED, UPDATE_UNTRUSTED, SCHEMA_INCOMPATIBLE and BACKUP_REQUIRED block transition.
Fresh origins/cleared storage cannot know a previously accepted maximum sequence; signed-but-old releases may appear valid until expiry and clocks are attacker/user influenced.
A same-origin XSS or compromised verifier defeats in-app checks.
Maintain independent recovery bundles rather than promising IPFS availability or rollback prevention on first use.

Test two CID origins and two gateways with real IndexedDB isolation, changed-origin backup restore, private browsing storage loss, stale manifest, lower sequence, forged rotation and modified JavaScript checker.
Confirm no secrets in update URLs and no direct fallback in strict mode.
Fetch/recompute CID and asset digests from both pin services.

Deploy one reviewed static release and separately verified EVM and Solana escrows to a selected test network; support frontend rollback without pretending immutable funded terms or public artifacts can be rolled back; and give an operator a procedure to recover funds directly from chain state when the frontend, origin or gateway is unavailable.

In scope: reproducible build of the static client, escrow deployment to local or test networks, release manifest signing, static and IPFS publication, frontend rollback, and direct-contract fund recovery.
requirements.scopeNote: Existing local/native EVM or display-only primitives are related evidence only; this source clause requires the still-open actual browser/live/native-family integration.

requirements.text: Out of scope: mainnet promotion, real-funds enablement (`RELEASE_ENABLED` stays 0), fiat recovery, arbitration-enabled escrow (Phase 6), and any claim of independent audit.
Testnet deployment precedes independent real-funds release review; this runbook does not replace that review.
Applicability: no ZK circuit applies to G25.
Smart contract and program deployment applies: the EVM escrow (G17/G18, H2) and the Solana escrow program (H3).
This document authors no contract source; it defines how already-reviewed artifacts are deployed, recorded and used for recovery.
Two release sequences run independently.
The frontend sequence is a series of signed static manifests.
The chain sequence is a set of deployment records, one per network and escrow identity.
A frontend change never redeploys or re-keys an escrow.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SRC[Reviewed source commit] --> BLD[Reproducible build x2 builders]
    BLD --> DIG{Digests equal?}
    DIG -- no --> STOP[Stop: do not sign]
    DIG -- yes --> MAN[Sign release manifest, sequence N]
    MAN --> PUB[Publish static origin + IPFS CID]
    PUB --> VER[Client verifies manifest before use]
    CHN[Escrow build] --> TNET[Deploy to test network]
    TNET --> REC[DeploymentRecord]
    REC --> REG[Signed deployment registry, G11]
    REG --> MAN
```
DeploymentRecord (one per network and escrow instance):
`{releaseManifestDigest, chainId, genesisIdentity, contractOrProgramId, codeDigest, initializationTx, authorityModel, assetAllowlistDigest, rpcPolicyDigest, explorerTemplate, reviewEvidenceDigest}`
- `chainId` and `genesisIdentity` are read from the node, never from configuration alone.
- `codeDigest` is the EVM runtime code hash or the Solana program data hash, read from chain state after deployment.
- `authorityModel` is one of `immutable` (EVM, no admin functions) or `upgradeable(authority)` (Solana).
A record with an unknown or hidden authority is invalid.
- `assetAllowlistDigest` covers the native asset and the allowlisted ERC-20 or SPL/Token-2022 mints only.
ReleaseManifest (signed, monotonic `sequence`):
`{sequence, releaseId, sourceCommit, builderDigests[], files[{path, sha256, bytes}], storageSchema, deploymentRegistryDigest, minReaderSchema, advisory?}`
Storage compatibility: `storageSchema` must be readable by the client that receives the manifest.
A client that sees a schema newer than it supports refuses to write and offers read-only export (`SCHEMA_TOO_NEW`).

Recovery package (published with every release, usable without the frontend): ABI (EVM) and IDL (Solana), addresses and code hashes per network, exact release and refund parameter encoding, chain-time instructions, and the receipt and journal formats.
The package contains no wallet private keys, seeds or passphrases.
Check out the reviewed commit by full SHA.
Record `sourceCommit`.
Install from the lockfile only: `npm ci --ignore-scripts`.
The Node major is 24 (`engines.node` in `package.json`).
Record the exact Node and npm versions.
Run `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run check:specs` and `npm run test:browser`.
A failure stops the release.
Build the static client with a fixed environment.
No build-time network access is used except the pinned dependency fetch in step 2.
Two independent builders (different machines or operators) produce the artifact.
Compare SHA-256 of every file.
Any difference stops signing.
Record both builder digests.
Generate `files[]` with sha256 and byte counts.
The archive order is sorted by path.
Primary reference for the static output layout: [Vite static deployment](https://vite.dev/guide/static-deploy).

requirements.text: Primary references: [Solana program deployment](https://solana.com/docs/programs/deploying); [Ethereum JSON-RPC](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/apis/json-rpc/).
- The release key is held offline or in a hardware-backed signer controlled by the maintainers.
It is never stored in the repository, CI logs or the build output.
- Sign the canonical JSON of the manifest.
The signature covers `sequence`, all file digests, `storageSchema` and `deploymentRegistryDigest`.

- A client accepts a manifest only if `sequence` is strictly greater than the last accepted sequence, the signature verifies against the trust root bundled in the release, and every fetched file matches its digest.
- The first release after any key compromise uses an out-of-band trust re-bootstrap (see G26).
A same-origin unsigned replacement key is never accepted.
Upload the verified files to the static origin.
Record origin URL and upload time (UTC).
Pin the same files to IPFS.
Record the root CID and confirm that a second gateway returns identical bytes for each path.
Publish the manifest and recovery package beside the files, and record both digests in the release log.
Smoke-test from a clean profile: load the origin, verify the manifest signature, and confirm the displayed `releaseId`.
Old immutable artifacts and old CIDs are never overwritten or removed by the release process.
Promotion happens only after G24 end-to-end evidence and G15 manifest checks pass for the new `sequence`.
Rollback means publishing a new manifest with a higher `sequence` built from a previously reviewed `sourceCommit`.
It does not reuse the old sequence number and does not edit any published file.
The rollback manifest must:
- carry a `storageSchema` the current clients can read (storage downgrade is forbidden);
- reference the current `deploymentRegistryDigest` (escrow addresses and deadlines are unchanged by rollback);
- disable new funding in an advisory where needed (see G26).
Clients on an incompatible newer schema keep their data and offer read-only export.
Existing escrow addresses and deadlines stay unchanged.
Maintainers can disable new funding in the UI but cannot pause immutable on-chain settlement.
This procedure works with no frontend, origin or gateway, using only the recovery package and an external wallet or CLI.
Obtain the recovery package from at least two independent locations and compare the code hashes and addresses.
Connect to the network, confirm `chainId` and genesis identity, and confirm the code hash at the escrow address against `codeDigest`.
Read the escrow state directly from chain.
Record seller, buyer, asset, amount and deadline as stored on chain.
Do not trust the receipt for these values.
Compare the deadline with chain time (the latest block timestamp), never the local clock.
If chain time is before the deadline and you are the seller: construct the release transaction from the recovery package and submit it through your wallet.
If chain time is at or after the deadline: anyone may construct the refund, which pays the seller only.
Construct it and submit it.
Wait for finality, re-read the escrow state, and record the transaction hash and the final state.
Receipts are a discovery aid, not custody authority.
A receipt that disagrees with chain state is wrong.

Each operator action in this runbook produces an evidence entry with: operator identity, UTC timestamp, exact input digests, expected result, actual result, an independent witness, and actual chain evidence (transaction hash, block number, and read-back of the state).
An entry without a witness is recorded as unwitnessed.

Recovery interface (client, when available): `recoverTrade(receipt)` verifies network and code hash, reads the authoritative escrow, shows the bound seller, buyer, asset and deadline, and constructs the release or refund for an external wallet to sign.
The client does not hold keys.
A seller can release only before expiry.
Anyone can trigger a refund after expiry, and it pays only the seller.
Non-frontend interface: the recovery package provides explicit CLI or explorer instructions with the verified ABI or IDL and a privacy disclosure stating which public chain data the operator reads.
Error handling in the interface: `WRONG_NETWORK`, `CODE_MISMATCH`, `SCHEMA_TOO_NEW`, `RPC_UNAVAILABLE` and `STATE_UNCERTAIN` stop transaction construction until resolved.
- `WRONG_NETWORK`: the wallet or RPC is on a different chain than the record.
Stop; switch networks; do not sign.
- `CODE_MISMATCH`: the on-chain code hash differs from `codeDigest`.
Stop; treat the address as unverified; escalate to G26.
- `SCHEMA_TOO_NEW`: the client cannot write the stored schema.
Export read-only; do not downgrade.
- `RPC_UNAVAILABLE`: use an alternate endpoint from the signed registry only.
Do not use an unlisted endpoint.
- `STATE_UNCERTAIN`: a broadcast whose outcome is unknown.
Reconcile through the journal and chain before any retry.
A second submission without reconciliation risks a duplicate economic action.
Residual threats that frontend rollback cannot address:
- It cannot reverse transactions, recover fiat, or remove old CIDs from IPFS gateways.
- An untrusted origin can serve a dishonest recovery page.
The recovery package and section 4.6 must remain usable without it.
- A compromised release key can sign a malicious manifest until the trust re-bootstrap completes (G26).
- Seller-side loss of the wallet before expiry leaves the escrow for refund after deadline only.
Rehearsals required before any test-network record is accepted:
Gateway outage: the origin serves the release and IPFS is unreachable.
Clients load from origin.
Bad frontend promotion: publish a deliberately broken sequence on a test origin, then roll back with a higher sequence.
Confirm clients reject the broken build by digest and accept the rollback.
Schema-forward-only state: open a profile written by a newer schema and confirm read-only export and no write.
Lost origin: run section 4.6 with no frontend, using only the downloaded recovery package, on both chain families.
Unavailable primary RPC: confirm fallback to registry-listed endpoints and `RPC_UNAVAILABLE` when none respond.
Wallet account change mid-trade: confirm transaction construction stops and re-reads the escrow for the new account.
Execute section 4.6 from the downloaded independent bundle on both chain families using test funds only.
Record measured recovery steps, elapsed time, finalized transactions and independent observer results.
Record each rehearsal in the evidence record with exact revisions pinned.
Release remains blocked until independent security review and all chain-specific gates pass.
No rehearsal in this document has been performed.

Primary references (exact implementation revisions must be pinned in the evidence record): [Vite deployment](https://vite.dev/guide/static-deploy); [Solana program deployment](https://solana.com/docs/programs/deploying); [Ethereum JSON-RPC](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/apis/json-rpc/).
Represent validated application observations without mistaking a local event for a signed protocol message or authoritative settlement.
This envelope is internal to the app; Nostr events, chain logs and wallet requests retain their native formats.
Schema dispatch requires the source/kind pair: chain/chain-snapshot, relay/order-observed, wallet/wallet-invalidated, journal/intent-updated.
No other combination is accepted.
`TradeBinding` comes from CTX01; source payload contracts come from G08/G10/G12 and relay specifications.
Events without a trade binding (e.g. global route loss) use service-specific callbacks and are not forged into a trade envelope.
Validate exact object keys, version, source/kind, nonnegative safe integers, canonical event ID, binding and kind-specific data before dispatch.
Bound the complete serialized envelope to 64 KiB; large content belongs in a validated encrypted vault record referenced by opaque ID.
No event may carry raw keys, passphrases, proof witnesses or arbitrary diagnostics.
Use UTF-8 JSON for local persistence; no event-envelope hashing or signing algorithm is defined here.
IDs deduplicate local dispatch only and are not proof of authenticity.
A session-scoped dispatcher keeps at most 4096 recently seen event IDs in FIFO order.
Duplicate IDs are ignored.
Eviction permits old IDs to appear again, so reducers MUST also be idempotent based on source-native IDs and authority state.
Generation mismatch rejects stale events.
Sequence numbers order observations within the relevant source and binding, never across independent peers.
A local observedAt cannot decide order expiry, chain finality or event authority.
`dispatch` runs schema validation, then freshness checks, then the pure G08 reducer.
It emits no network calls and cannot sign transactions.
Reset clears bounded dedup state and subscribers; new generation is greater than the prior generation.
Sequence exhaustion or generation exhaustion at Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER requires session recreation, not wraparound.
Persistent intent sequencing uses G12 atomic vault revisions; it is not reset by a UI component remount.
Unknown future versions return `invalid` and do not partially apply data.
Injected source labels do not prove chain origin: only the corresponding bundled adapter can construct a validated internal observation after native verification.
Treat arbitrary imported envelope JSON as untrusted data, never as a direct reducer action.
Duplicate suppression does not prevent replay of protocol messages; native Nostr/chain/domain replay rules remain mandatory.
Unbounded IDs/payloads could exhaust memory; apply byte/count limits before enqueueing.
No cross-source last-writer-wins policy is allowed for money or escrow state.

Test every source/kind combination, unknown fields, negative/unsafe sequences, ID encoding, 64 KiB boundary, 4096-entry eviction, duplicate delivery, generation changes, reordered requests and future versions.
Reapply an event after dedup eviction and ensure no economic side effect.
A valid relay-sourced event cannot finalize escrow.
Fuzz 10000 bounded input envelopes per deterministic seed.

Dependencies: [system context](spec-system-context-contract.md), [state authority](../module_0.4.4_state_management/spec-client-state-authority.md), [transaction journal](../../../01_P2P_SHIELDED_OFFRAMP_ENGINE/feature_1.7_transaction_recovery/module_1.7.1_transaction_journal/spec-transaction-lifecycle-journal.md).
Define which subsystem may establish each fact in the basic noncustodial trade.
This contract governs the static off-ramp client.
The separate `payments/` custodial ledger branch is not an off-ramp dependency and MUST NOT be wired into wallet balance or settlement authority.
Server accounts, operator-held wallet keys, automated bank transfers, and privileged escrow release are outside the basic product.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U["Trader"] --> C["Static client"]
  C --> W["External wallet"]
  C --> R["Discovery and message relays"]
  W --> E["Versioned escrow"]
  C --> Q["Configured chain RPC"]
  C --> V["Encrypted local vault"]
```
| Fact | Authority | Cached or untrusted input |
| Spending consent | External wallet for current account/network | Button click, local journal |
| Funded, released, refunded | Supported deployed escrow, reconciled through configured RPC and finality policy | Relay event, receipt screenshot |
| Offer intent | Validated signed advertisement, still revalidated before funding | Relay ordering and availability |
| Fiat receipt | Seller's manual attestation in basic mode | Buyer statement, chat, screenshot, proof-provider output |
| Local recovery material | Authenticated G02 vault snapshot | localStorage, imported filenames |
| Privacy coverage | Per-channel enforceable G05 routing evidence | A selected UI preset |
RPCs can lie or censor; finality here means the chain adapter's observed policy, not independently verified consensus.
The UI MUST expose the RPC origin and unavailable/stale state.
Independent proof or light-client verification is a separate capability.
Start in locked/watch-only mode.
Load a validated network/deployment registry before wallet operations.
Treat every relay, RPC, wallet callback, backup, URL, and QR as untrusted input; validate at the boundary and enforce size limits before allocation or crypto.
Bind every economic command to `(chain family, network ID, deployment ID, trade ID, account generation)`; a mismatch invalidates the command before signing.
A wallet/network change cancels pending preparation and requires a new explicit confirmation.
An already broadcast transaction remains in the journal for reconciliation under its original binding.
The basic escrow seller can release only before its immutable deadline; timeout returns crypto to seller.
A fiat-paid assertion never grants release authority.
No extension may change already-funded terms.
With advanced packages removed, the basic client MUST still reconcile, release, refund, and export recovery information.
No chain or relay failure can be treated as proof that a transaction failed.
No cryptographic primitive or ZK circuit is defined by this boundary contract.
All command constructors take a validated binding and generation.
Missing deployment, unsupported chain, unavailable RPC, stale observation, and mismatched wallet return explicit refusal.
A renderer may display cached data while offline but MUST disable economic actions until fresh chain reconciliation.
Neither observedAt nor the local clock establishes escrow expiry; adapters use chain time.
A malicious relay can advertise a fake escrow address: accept deployment identity only from the validated registry, never the ad.
A compromised RPC can fabricate balances: show the trust boundary, use configured independent corroboration where supported, and refuse on observed disagreement.
An XSS attacker can read unlocked state and alter signing requests: G04 rendering/CSP and wallet confirmation remain required.
A dishonest seller can receive fiat and withhold release; the client must state this before payment.
TLS, encrypted chat, and ZK receipt evidence do not solve that basic economic risk.
Local backups cannot reverse chain outcomes or recover lost external-wallet spending keys.
Unit cases MUST cover each authority row, unknown chain/deployment, account/network changes before and after broadcast, and buyer fiat assertions with no authority.
Integration cases MUST remove all optional packages and exercise complete basic release/refund recovery.
Adversarial fixtures MUST include a validly signed ad with an unauthorized deployment, lying RPC responses, and stale local success after a simulated reorg.
Test both chain families before claiming parity.
No supported provider/browser/deployment matrix is approved by this spec alone.
